description: An agent that stopped to ask RESUMES with its saved context when the answer arrives inside this window
note: the principle - resume rather than restart - is Yakov's; the number was an Interface proposal, approved at #5200 and changeable here. AND the clock does not run while the resuming agent waits for a slot (Yakov #5358) - front-of-queue is not preemption, so a queue wait could otherwise eat the window and cold-restart an agent whose answer arrived in time

description: Past the resume window the agent is RESTARTED with the answer instead of resumed
note: the same boundary read from the other side - one value, stated twice on purpose so neither reading needs arithmetic

description: A suspended agent still without an answer is BLOCKED
Where a resuming agent re-enters the queue
note: not a number - a position; front or back are the only values

description: A run is killed after this long with NO output at all. The clock starts when the process comes up and resets on every line
note: there is no wall-clock limit on a task. NO CLOCK RUNS WHILE A RUN IS WAITING - not for a dispatch slot and not for the Claude seat (Yakov #5358). The silence clock starts when the run actually begins producing, because a run queued for the seat is a live process with nothing to say, and killing it for that would be killing it for waiting

description: Last-resort liveness check, and only when no run is live or the slot is held
note: asks whether the process exists; the silence-kill asks whether it is producing anything. Two mechanisms, never merged

description: How many attempts run without Yakov. Beyond this the issue waits for his word
note: there is no ceiling on the NUMBER of attempts - only on how many run without him. It counts ROUNDS OF THE FLOW and never a script's own internal retries - the two counters are deliberately separate and neither counts the other (Yakov #5251)

description: How many dispatched runs may be LIVE at once. Engine-blind: the dispatch engine never knows and never asks which engine a run will land on
note: the ONLY capacity statement in the specification. It counts dispatched runs, nothing else - the Orchestrator's own judgment calls are not dispatched tasks and are not counted here. It is NOT the Claude seat: the seat is one concurrent session on the subscription, it is not ours, it is not a dial, and it is enforced inside the shared queue after routing has chosen - never by the Orchestrator, which is forbidden to ask which engine a run gets. Throughput is therefore (runs off Claude, genuinely parallel) + (runs on Claude, one at a time), and the mix is a routing decision, not a value here

description: A status write to Linear is retried this many times before it is surfaced
note: a status write is STATE - lost, it strands an issue holding the slot

description: A comment is sent once and never retried
note: a comment is a MESSAGE - lost, it costs information, not correctness. The asymmetry with status writes is deliberate

description: How many times a DETERMINISTIC step retries its own operation before it reports failure - a dropped IMAP connection, a timed-out request
note: the step's own retry belongs to the step's owner; the flow loop counts rounds of the FLOW. Two counters, two meanings, and neither counts the other - which is what stops three script tries times two flow attempts becoming six. The number is an Interface proposal and is meant to be changed here

description: How long a task claim stays valid without a heartbeat refresh. Past it the claim is dead and the issue may be recovered
note: three missed heartbeats at the 5-minute interval. This is what lets recovery tell a LIVE worker from a dead one - under parallelism the old inference "nothing else is dispatching, so an In Progress issue was cut off" is false and would revert live work

description: The priority the Orchestrator's own judgment calls take in the shared queue
note: not a number - a position, the same value the Interface holds. Without it the Orchestrator queues BEHIND agents it dispatched itself, and while it waits the single dispatch loop cannot dispatch, close or render anything. Priority inversion, and it exists only under parallelism. Non-preemptive as always: it waits at most one in-flight run

description: How many question-and-answer rounds one agent-to-agent conversation may run before the issue goes to Yakov
note: The count is DERIVED from the issue tag-attachment history and is never stored in a field (Yakov #5666) - a stored counter is a counter someone forgets to update. Two agents at most, always: the cap bounds the ROUNDS, not the participants. Raised from 3 to 4 on Yakov #5709, together with the loop ceilings, so the two do not disagree.

description: Longest plain-text piece the bridge puts in one Telegram message before splitting
note: Headroom below Telegram's own 4096 cap for the [i/n] part marker AND for HTML expansion, measured at 1.21-1.22x on a densely formatted Hebrew message. Telegram's 4096 is deliberately NOT a row here - it is their limit, not our decision

description: How much of a replied-to message is passed through to the agent
note: When a passage is highlighted the passage is sent instead of the whole message (Yakov #4937); this bounds both

description: Largest file the bridge will download from Telegram
note: = 20 MB. Telegram's getFile ceiling, stated as ours because refusing earlier is a policy choice

description: Above this the turn carries a visible warning that recall is degrading and the agent may overwrite its own earlier statements
note: The warning sits on its own line immediately above the signature

description: Minimum gap between two Telegram alerts about the same unauthorized (kind, user)
note: Stops a repeated prober from flooding the group

description: Minimum gap between two Linear security issues about the same unauthorized user
note: Longer than the Telegram debounce on purpose: an issue is durable and Yakov-routed, so a persistent prober must not flood Linear

description: Timeout on an ordinary Telegram API call
Timeout on downloading a file from Telegram
note: Larger than the API timeout because the payload is the file itself

description: Timeout on uploading a voice reply
Timeout on a bridge-spawned helper process (session reconcile, session namer)
note: These shell out precisely so a failure can never hang the poll loop; the timeout is the last guarantee of that

description: Timeout on a cockpit subprocess call
How many incoming message timestamps are kept for the crossed-in-transit check
note: Paired with incoming_ts_trim

description: How many of the oldest timestamps are dropped once incoming_ts_memory is exceeded
note: Paired with incoming_ts_memory; split into its own row because a table row holds one value

description: Ceiling on how many queued messages a single STOP drains
note: Effectively unbounded in normal use; it is a guard against a runaway loop, not a policy on queue size

description: Wall-clock cap on ONE bash tool call inside the agentic loop
note: The widest tool, so the longest cap. A run may make many such calls; this bounds each one, not the run

description: Cap on one grep tool call
Cap on one glob tool call
Cap on the per-tool-call permission check that runs before every tool call
note: Sits in front of EVERY tool call, so it is on the hot path twice per step

description: Cap on a file read performed as the agent's own OS user
Cap on a file write performed as the agent's own OS user
Cap on the PDF page-count probe that decides heavy vs cheap extraction tool
Cap on the notify.sh call that sends a proactive routing alert
note: Deliberately short: an alert that cannot be sent must not delay the routing decision it describes

description: Cap on the OpenRouter key-metadata call (remaining credit / rate limits)
note: Deliberately NOT the per-engine http_timeout_s: this is a metadata call, not a completion

description: How many times a blank model turn is re-forced before the step gives up
The same tool call repeated N times in a row counts as stagnation
note: One of four independent stagnation shapes

description: An A-B-A-B oscillation over N calls counts as stagnation
note: One of four independent stagnation shapes

description: An A-B-C-A-B-C oscillation over N calls counts as stagnation
note: One of four independent stagnation shapes

description: N identical tool OUTPUTS in a row counts as stagnation, even when the calls differ
note: The only one of the four that watches results rather than calls

description: Calling the SAME nonexistent tool N times ends the run as a capability gap
note: Paired with missing_tool_total_limit

description: Calling ANY nonexistent tools N times in total ends the run as a capability gap
note: Paired with missing_tool_same_name_limit

description: The point in the run where the model is told to stop exploring and converge
note: Paired with wrapup_nudge_min_steps

description: Below this max_steps the wrap-up nudge is skipped entirely
note: A short run has no room for a mid-course correction; nudging it would only cost a step

description: After a trim, how far below the budget the conversation is cut back to
note: Hysteresis: trimming exactly to the budget would re-trigger on the very next turn

description: A conversation this short or shorter is never trimmed, whatever its byte size
note: Protects the system message plus the task from being evicted by their own size

description: Share of the tool-output cap reserved for stderr: cap divided by this
note: Paired with stderr_share_floor, whichever is larger

description: Minimum stderr kept regardless of the tool-output cap
note: Paired with stderr_share_divisor; guarantees an error message survives a small cap

description: How many conversation turns are carried to the next engine when a run escalates
note: Paired with handoff_per_turn_chars

description: Per-turn character budget inside that handoff package
note: Paired with handoff_max_turns

description: How much of the task text is sent to the pre-flight triage gate
note: WHICH ENGINE serves triage is a routing decision and lives in task_routing_rules.csv, not here

description: Output cap on the pre-flight triage call
note: Raised 400 -> 1500 on 2026-08-30 after a live run: the gate is served by a REASONING model, whose thinking tokens count against this cap, and a real answer measured 339 completion tokens. At 400 the JSON truncated mid-object, rfind("}") found no closing brace, and the gate returned None -- failing open on exactly the tasks that had most to say. Still far cheaper than the 15-30 loop steps it exists to save.

description: Minimum gap between repeats of the same overflow or override alert
Lookback window for the weekly Claude token budget
note: backlog_threshold and weekly_max_tokens themselves are already external, in engines/overflow.json

description: Step ceiling on the LIVE conversation path, which overrides engine_adapters.csv's per-engine max_steps
note: Declared 2026-08-30 to make an existing silent override visible. Dispatched work keeps the per-engine table value; a live conversation is different work and gets a higher ceiling. Behaviour unchanged by this row

description: Exponential growth factor between HTTP retries: backoff * base**attempt
note: Distinct from engine_adapters.csv's retry_backoff_s, which is the FIRST wait; this is how it grows

description: Silence window for a Claude-CLI subprocess: kill it only if it has produced NO output for this long. Not a total time limit -- a long tool-using run that keeps printing is never cut.
note: Was SILENCE = int(os.environ.get("RUN_AGENT_SILENCE", "600")) -- a compiled default AND an env override, two more sources for one number. Both deleted; this row is the only source. Value carried over unchanged from the constant it replaces.

description: Absolute wall-clock ceiling for a Claude-CLI subprocess, regardless of output. 0 = OFF, and off is the deliberate default: the silence window above is the real guard, and a hard ceiling would kill a long, healthy, still-producing run.
note: Was MAX_WALL = int(os.environ.get("RUN_AGENT_MAX", "0")). Same two-sources problem as the row above. 0 is meaningful here, not empty -- it is the switch that turns the ceiling off.

description: Ceiling on one run's checkpoint store. Crossing it stops the run and alerts instead of filling the disk.
read_by: the runtime, before each checkpoint write
note: Added after a runaway loop wrote a 90 GB checkpoint database on 2026-08-31 and took the server to 93% full.

description: Hard ceiling on how many graph steps ONE run may execute, loops included. It is the backstop above every per-step loop_ceiling: a 48-step flow whose loops all run to their limit stays far below it, and a routing bug that would otherwise spin for ever hits it and stops.
read_by: the runtime, as the graph recursion limit on every invoke and resume
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6490
note: The 2026-08-31 runaway that wrote 90 GB of checkpoints had no ceiling of this kind. Per-step loop_ceiling bounds ONE loop; this bounds the whole run.

description: How long ONE Telegram long-poll waits before asking again. This is the worst-case delay between Yakov pressing a button and the run moving. Measured 2026-08-31 at 25 seconds: the answered gates showed waits of 24, 40 and 51 seconds - multiples of the cycle, not of Yakov. Three seconds costs about twenty requests a minute, far inside Telegram's limits, and makes the button feel immediate.
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6534
note: Telegram's own getUpdates long-poll ceiling is 50s; 25 keeps a stop responsive.

description: How long a run waits at a human gate before it stops waiting and leaves the run paused on disk. The run is NOT cancelled - the checkpoint holds, and resuming it later is one command.
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6490
note: A gate is a human decision; the default is a full day so a night does not kill a run.

description: Ceiling on one engine call made through the single engine wrapper.
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6490

description: Largest single file the artifact store accepts on the host. Above it the run stops and asks, rather than silently parking something enormous.
note: Heavy files never enter git; this bounds what enters the host store too.

description: The file-size gate: no file this large or larger may enter a commit on the runtime repository.
note: This is the gate that stops a render or a CAD export slipping into the repository.

description: How many times ONE agent step may go round the think-call-a-tool-read-the-result loop before it must answer. The step ends with whatever it has; it is never cut off silently - the record says the ceiling was reached.
read_by: the agent loop in the engine wrapper
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6506
note: Bounds cost and time per step. The run_step_ceiling bounds the whole run; this bounds one step inside it.

description: Ceiling on one local tool call - a fetch, a file write, a read.
ruling: Interface proposal during the phase A build, #6506

description: Which human gates of a run answer themselves instead of stopping for Yakov. Empty = every gate asks. Yakov #6809: cancel the six least important, so a full design-robot run costs six answers and not twelve. Two of those six - 17 and 39, the outbound-email gates - stopped existing when Yakov #6801/#6812 replaced the supplier emails with a web search and CAD modelling, so only four numbers remain here and the run still costs six answers. THE RULE BEHIND THE SIX: a gate that only CONFIRMS what a step already wrote is cancelled, because the file is on disk and in the trace and can be read after the run; a gate that FORKS the run - what continues, what is pruned, what goes to CAD - is kept. Two of the six (17, 39) are the outbound-email gates and cost nothing at all in a run that sends no mail. Kept: 4 the mission, 13 and 22 the alternatives, 28 the simulation prune, 37 the selection for CAD, 46b the design lock.
note: This is a RUN setting, not a change to the flow: the 48 canonical rows stay exactly as ruling 17 requires. A cancelled gate is still executed and still recorded - stamped actor=auto, provenance=unattended - so the trace never pretends a human decided. Restoring any one of them is deleting its number from this cell.

description: Which route a flow row marked `difficulty=high` is given. Everything else keeps the route of its own agent row. THE POINT OF THIS ROW: the flow declares how HARD the work is - a property of the work - and the routing layer alone turns hardness into a model. The flow never learns a model name, so the iron rule holds: the agent engine never asks for a specific model.
note: The ten high rows of design-robot, chosen by one rule - expensive wherever a mistake is not caught later: 3 the capability list, 9 propose alternatives, 11 filter against the spec, 14 select chassis/wheels/drive/gripper, 20 choose parts, 25 make them better, 29 cross-check combinations, 31 apply the simulation conclusions, 39 model from a picture, 43a the final CAD. Runners-up not taken: 34 and 42. Cost: sol is 4/20 per M against luna's 0.2/1.2, about 17x, so the ten rows dominate the bill and the other 24 are nearly free.

description: How much SKILL text an agent carries in its system prompt. The prompt is paid for on every turn of every step, so this is the dial between an agent that knows our methods and a bill that grows with the number of turns. 12000 characters is roughly three full skills. It is deliberately generous for the first real run, where the point is the quality of the deliverable; if the bill argues otherwise, this cell is the one place to argue back.
note: Overflow is ANNOUNCED inside the prompt itself, never silently dropped.

description: Whether the Interface reads every step's deliverable before the next step begins. Yakov #6842: it judges whether the work is accurate enough, and if it is not it does NOT send it back - the run never goes backwards. It writes an instruction that makes the NEXT step sharper, and the flow carries on.
note: Deliberately not a loop and not a branch in the graph: a redo would double the cost of the expensive steps and could not terminate on its own. One short forward-only call is the cheap shape of the same idea. A review that throws is swallowed and recorded - it must never be what kills a run.

description: How long the note a review may hand to the next step. Short on purpose: it is an instruction, not a second opinion, and it is paid for again in every prompt that carries it forward.
note: A review with nothing to say answers OK and costs one line; only a real remark is carried.

description: Whether a run writes its own closing report when it ends. Yakov #6847: three sections - what to change in the FLOW table, what to change in the CONTENT the agents produced, and the whole thing with every improvement worth making, most valuable first, each with its cost.
note: Written from what the run already produced - the running critique the between-step reviews wrote, the trace, and what the record measured - so it costs ONE call and invents nothing. It runs on the high-difficulty route on purpose: it is the one artefact a human reads end to end. A run that walked no step writes none, and a report that throws is recorded and never kills the run.

description: The route for the two JUDGEMENT roles - the review between steps and the closing report (#6868). **Claude on the Max subscription, and NOTHING ELSE** (#6881). Yakov asked for the Max subscription and did not ask for GPT here; a cascade to GPT was the Interface's own addition and is removed. If the Max seat is not free the review does not happen and the run carries on without it.
note: A single route, deliberately not a cascade. The run waits `claude_seat_wait_seconds` for the seat and then MOVES ON without a review for that step - it never blocks, and it never quietly substitutes a different engine for a judgement Yakov asked Claude to make. A missed review is recorded as such.

description: How long a run waits for the Max seat before giving up on a judgement call and carrying on without it (#6881: three minutes). The seat is held only while the Telegram bridge is composing a reply to Yakov, so three minutes covers almost any single answer.
note: Giving up means the step has no review. It does NOT mean another engine writes one.
